title: Tunneling-mode NEMS access switch: vacuum gap replaces the leaky channel
idea: Start from the lowest-leakage switch physics allows: a vacuum gap, where off-current falls about 10x per angstrom of tunneling distance. Replace the access MOSFET with an electrostatically pulled 3 nm SiC nanobeam in a hermetically sealed cavity that moves from a 4 nm gap to a ~0.5 nm non-contact tunneling gap. It never touches, so there is no stiction or wear. Near-gap tunneling easily supplies the ~0.5 uA a 5 fF write in 10 ns needs, while the open-gap current is below 1e-21 A.
why: Removes subthreshold, GIDL and junction leakage in one move, so the 13 fA tail (fact 3) disappears. Retention becomes limited by the capacitor dielectric (minutes to hours), cutting refresh energy and the 10-20% bandwidth tax by >100x.

title: Junction-free Ga2O3 back-end access transistor at 4.8 eV bandgap
idea: Intrinsic generation scales as n_i ~ exp(-Eg/2kT), so go past IGZO (~3.2 eV) to ALD amorphous or nanocrystalline Ga2O3 (~4.8 eV). Build n-channel thin-film access transistors below 400 C above the periphery, with no p-n junction at the storage node, and suppress oxygen-vacancy traps with an N2O plasma plus an Al2O3 cap. The only leak paths left are gate-dielectric tunneling and deep-trap emission, and film thickness controls both.
why: Adding 1.6 eV of gap lowers n_i by exp(-1.6/0.052), about 1e-13, so retention becomes capacitor-limited (>1000 s) and refresh nearly vanishes (fact 3). BEOL stacking needs no EUV front-end steps and supports 3D tiers (facts 2, 4).

title: Lattice-matched GaP storage-node junction starves GIDL and SRH generation
idea: Silicon's 1.12 eV gap is what makes band-to-band tunneling at the gate-drain overlap easy. Regrow only the storage-node contact as 5-10 nm n+ GaP (2.26 eV, 0.37% lattice mismatch to Si) by selective MOCVD. The high-field overlap and the metallurgical junction then lie in wide-gap material, while the channel stays silicon for drive current.
why: BTBT rate ~ exp(-B*Eg^1.5/F), so doubling Eg multiplies the exponent about 2.9x and cuts GIDL by >1e5 at equal field. SRH generation in the GaP volume falls ~1e9 through n_i. Together they attack the GIDL/TAT-dominated 13 fA tail for an estimated 4-10x longer refresh interval (fact 3).

title: 200 K cool-not-cryo DRAM retargets Vt to cut wordline voltage
idea: At 200 K the Boltzmann limit falls from 60 to 40 mV/dec, and junction generation (Ea ~0.6 eV) is ~5e6 lower than at 85 C. Run memory sleds at 200 K with single-stage vapor-compression cooling. Spend the leakage windfall by lowering access-transistor Vt by about a third, so at equal Ioff wordline VPP drops from ~3 V to ~2 V and the array from ~1.1 V to ~0.8 V.
why: Refresh essentially disappears (fact 3), and CV^2 wordline and array energy falls ~45-55% (fact 10) after paying a cooling COP of ~0.6 at 200 K. The device is retargeted from first principles instead of run cold as-is.

title: Bidirectional tunnel-FET pair sized to the 0.5 uA write budget
idea: Derive what the access device really needs: charging 5 fF by 1 V in 10 ns takes only I = CV/t ~0.5 uA, which a vertical GaSb/InAs or SiGe/Si heterojunction tunnel FET can supply. TFETs conduct in one direction, so stack two opposite-oriented vertical TFETs in one pillar, one for write and one for read. In the off state the band-to-band window is closed, with a sub-60 mV/dec slope.
why: This escapes thermionic Boltzmann leakage. Over a 0.6 V gate window, a 30 mV/dec average swing gives ~1e10 lower Ioff than a MOSFET at equal Ion, pushing retention from 64 ms to seconds or more (fact 3).

title: Negative-capacitance HZO buried wordline trades swing for higher Vt
idea: Insert a ~3 nm ferroelectric Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 layer into the buried-wordline gate stack, capacitance-matched to the channel. The internal gate voltage is then amplified (body factor m<1), and swing drops to ~40-45 mV/dec in the operating window. Spend that gain on a higher Vt at the same Ion, not on lower voltage.
why: Over a 0.9 V gate window, going from 65 to 45 mV/dec cuts Ioff by about 10^(0.9/0.045 - 0.9/0.065), roughly 1e6, at equal Ion. Even a tenth of that removes the subthreshold part of the 13 fA tail (fact 3).

title: Self-dissolving silver filament as two-terminal crosspoint access element
idea: A diffusive Ag:SiO2 threshold switch grows a sub-nm Ag bridge above ~0.4 V. When bias drops, surface energy breaks the bridge up within ~100 ns, leaving a 2-5 nm insulating gap (ON/OFF ~1e9-1e10, slope <1 mV/dec). Put one in series with each capacitor in a 4F^2 1S1C crosspoint biased so half-selected cells never cross threshold.
why: The access device becomes a gap-limited switch with near-ideal steepness. It removes the transistor footprint (6F^2 to 4F^2) and junction leakage (fact 3). The core risk is endurance: ~1e10 cycles is demonstrated, and 1e15 or more is needed.

title: Monolayer WSe2 channel wrapped around the capacitor pillar sidewall
idea: Thermal generation scales with depleted semiconductor volume times n_i. A 0.7 nm monolayer has almost no volume and a gap of ~1.6-2 eV. Grow MOCVD WSe2 or MoS2 conformally (<500 C) on the outer sidewall of the vertical storage pillar with a ring wordline. The result is a gate-all-around vertical access device with no silicon body and a 4F^2 footprint.
why: Leakage drops ~1e6 from n_i and ~10x from volume, removing the junction and TAT tail sources (fact 3). It also gives a vertical, stackable cell (fact 2) with no lateral transistor.

title: Junctionless nanosheet access device removes the storage-node p-n junction
idea: Make the access transistor a uniformly n+ (~1e19 cm^-3) 5 nm nanosheet that the wordline workfunction fully depletes when off. Source, channel and storage node are then one doping type, so no reverse-biased metallurgical junction touches the storage node. A buried dielectric, not a p-well, isolates it from the substrate.
why: The dominant tail mechanism, SRH/TAT generation in the storage-junction depletion region, has no junction left to occur in. Negative off-bias controls the remaining subthreshold leakage. Expect ~10x tail compression and a correspondingly longer refresh interval (fact 3).

title: Negative-charge Al2O3 liner accumulates STI sidewalls against surface generation
idea: Borrow the passivation physics of PERC solar cells and backside-illuminated image sensors. Line the STI trenches next to storage nodes with 3-5 nm ALD Al2O3 carrying ~-3e12 cm^-2 fixed charge. This accumulates holes on the p-type sidewall and pushes the depletion region away from STI interface traps. Surface generation, which scales with Dit x n_i in depletion, falls by orders of magnitude once the surface is accumulated.
why: STI-edge cells are a known tail population. 10-100x lower surface generation gives ~4-10x longer worst-case retention for one ALD step and no new lithography (facts 3, 4).

title: Standby plate-line swing collapses storage-junction field during self-refresh
idea: Tail leakage is field-enhanced (trap-assisted tunneling ~ exp(gamma*sqrt(F))), so reduce the field instead of the conductance. On self-refresh entry, slowly ramp the shared cell plate down ~0.4 V. This couples every storage node down, so '1' cells sit closer to the p-well potential while '0' cells stay reverse-biased thanks to the negative p-well bias. Ramp the plate back before exit; its large capacitance is swung only twice per idle period.
why: A 0.4 V cut in junction reverse bias lowers field-enhanced tail current ~3-10x. That stretches self-refresh intervals by the same factor and cuts idle power 10-25% (fact 3).

title: Recombination-enhanced annealing pulses lock VRT defects in benign state
idea: Variable-retention-time cells come from metastable defects that flip between high- and low-generation configurations over a ~0.5-1 eV barrier. Periodically park a row's data in a spare row by in-DRAM copy, then pulse its bitlines ~0.3 V below the p-well for ~1 us to forward-bias the storage junctions, and write the data back. Injected minority carriers recombine at the defect, delivering ~1 eV per event to drive it into its low-leakage configuration (recombination-enhanced defect reaction).
why: VRT forces 2-4x refresh guardbands and makes retention profiling unsafe. Locking defects into the benign state would remove that guardband and make per-row refresh trustworthy (fact 3).

title: LC-resonant adiabatic refresh spends refresh's spare time, not energy
idea: A normal restore dissipates ~CV^2 because bitlines and wordlines are slammed in ~10 ns, yet refresh has a 64 ms window. Drive refresh-only activations with ~1 us ramps from an on-package LC tank or N-step tank capacitors. Dissipation then follows (RC/T)*CV^2, and most of the charge returns to the supply.
why: With T/RC ~50-100, the switching part of the ~46 fJ/bit refresh energy drops ~10x. That attacks refresh's 16-33% share of idle power (fact 3) without touching the cell.

title: Thin p-well with deep minority-carrier sink beneath the array
idea: Above ~70 C, diffusion current from carriers generated in the neutral p-well (Ea ~ Eg ~1.1 eV) overtakes depletion generation, and any electron generated within a diffusion length can wander into a storage node. Thin the array p-well to ~0.3 um and place a strongly biased buried n+ collector plane just below. Thermally generated electrons are swept away vertically before they reach storage nodes, the image-sensor vertical-overflow-drain trick.
why: The generation volume feeding storage nodes shrinks ~10-30x. This matters most in hot HBM stacks at 85-95 C, where refresh doubles. Expect a 2-5x retention gain at high temperature (facts 3, 6).

title: Charge-transfer pre-sensing lets cells lose 80 percent of charge
idea: Today the cell's ~30,000 electrons are diluted onto a ~50 fF bitline to give ~100 mV, yet the kT/C noise of a 2 fF node is only ~1.4 mV. Hold the bitline at a fixed potential with a transfer gate biased at threshold, so the cell's charge is funneled onto a ~2 fF sense node. This revives the 1970s charge-transfer amplifier with modern offset cancellation and multiplies the signal ~20x.
why: If 20% of the original charge is enough for a reliable read, retention = dQ/I grows ~4-5x with no change in leakage. Refresh energy and bandwidth fall in proportion (facts 1, 3).

title: Air-spacer drain overlap defuses the GIDL hot spot
idea: GIDL is set by the peak field where the wordline overlaps the storage-node junction, and it scales as exp(-B/F). Replace the gate dielectric in only the last ~5 nm of overlap with a sealed air spacer (k=1). This lowers the overlap field ~3-4x and leaves channel control untouched.
why: A 3x field cut lowers BTBT GIDL by several decades. GIDL is what limits deeper negative wordline off-bias, so this allows deeper off-bias and ~3-10x longer tail retention (fact 3). It also reduces wordline-to-node coupling relevant to row hammer (fact 9).

title: Van der Waals resonant-tunneling latch keeps each storage node topped up
idea: Integrate a series pair of graphene/hBN/graphene resonant-tunneling diodes (a Goto pair) in the capacitor top-electrode stack. Each storage node then has two stable voltages, and the RTD peak current continuously replaces what leaks away. The budget from first principles: peak current must exceed the 13 fA tail, and valley current must stay below ~0.7 pA per cell, the average power refresh spends per bit (46 fJ / 64 ms). The target is a peak-to-valley ratio of ~20 at the ~1 pA scale.
why: Refresh disappears entirely (fact 3) if BEOL-compatible 2D stacks meet the peak-to-valley target. Bistability becomes a property of the cell, not of the controller.

title: Carbon-cluster proximity gettering pulls metal traps from storage junctions
idea: Mid-gap metal impurities (Fe, Cu, Ni at ~1e10 cm^-3) are ideal SRH generation centers, and image sensors remove dark-current hot pixels with buried carbon-cluster gettering layers. Implant a C3H5 molecular cluster layer ~1 um under the array before the well anneals, so metals precipitate there, away from storage-node depletion regions.
why: SRH generation scales with trap density in the depletion region. Cutting metallic traps 10x compresses the leakage tail that sets the 64 ms interval (fact 3), for one implant step and no lithography.

title: Antiferroelectric back-switching plateau acts as a constant-voltage charge reservoir
idea: Add a thin antiferroelectric ZrO2 film in parallel with the storage dielectric. Size it so the written '1' voltage is above its field-induced polar switching and its back-switching edge sits just above the sense threshold. As leakage drains the node, the AFE back-switches and releases ~10-20 uC/cm^2 of polarization charge at a nearly constant voltage, pinning the node like a clamped reservoir.
why: Usable charge above the sense threshold rises several-fold without taller pillars. That attacks fact 1 and the retention equation t = dQ/I (fact 3), for 3-5x retention at equal leakage.

title: Post-fab Vt healing of tail access transistors via trap-layer programming
idea: Random dopant and trap fluctuations put a few transistors per billion 4-5 sigma low in Vt, and their subthreshold current dominates the tail. Add a thin SiN charge-trap layer in the buried-wordline liner. At wafer test, find the short-retention cells and inject electrons into only their gate stacks (high wordline voltage, their bitline driven, neighbors inhibited) to raise their Vt ~200 mV.
why: At ~70 mV/dec, +200 mV cuts a tail cell's subthreshold leakage ~700x. That collapses the distribution toward the median and allows a 4-8x longer refresh interval (fact 3).

title: Undoped channel with workfunction-set Vt shrinks the random-dopant tail
idea: A 12 nm access channel holds only ~50-100 dopant atoms, so Poisson fluctuation (sigma ~ sqrt(N)) gives sigma-Vt ~30-50 mV and a fat low-Vt tail. Remove channel doping and set Vt with a dipole-tuned workfunction metal (TiN with La or Al dipoles) in the buried wordline, as logic did with FinFETs. Sigma-Vt drops to ~10-15 mV, limited by metal grain granularity.
why: The refresh interval is set by the ~6-sigma cell. A 3x smaller sigma moves that cell ~150 mV closer to the median Vt, for ~100x less tail leakage and a 2-4x longer refresh interval using only logic's toolkit (fact 3).

title: Quantum-confined 3 nm silicon body widens the bandgap without new materials
idea: Confining silicon to a ~3 nm body raises its subband edges, so the effective gap grows ~0.2-0.3 eV. Because n_i ~ exp(-Eg/2kT), generation drops by about exp(-0.25/0.052), roughly 100x. Build the vertical access channel as an ultrathin crystalline silicon shell on a dielectric core (macaroni-style as in 3D NAND, crystallized by laser or lateral solid-phase epitaxy), so the whole depletion region around the storage node is confined.
why: This gives ~100x less thermal generation in silicon itself (fact 3) and fits existing deposition and anneal tools and vertical 3D cell concepts (fact 2).

title: Grounded shield rail kills passing-wordline leakage into storage nodes
idea: In buried-wordline arrays each storage node sits beside a neighboring row's 'passing' wordline. When that line pulses to ~3 V, its fringing field induces leakage and electron injection into the node, the same coupling behind row hammer. Insert a thin grounded conductive rail (doped poly or TiN) in the isolation trench between the passing wordline and the storage node to terminate the field lines.
why: This removes the access-dependent leakage that shortens effective retention under heavy traffic and raises the ~1k row-hammer threshold. Refresh then needs no guardband for neighbor activity (facts 3, 9).

title: Refresh-off banks for tensors that die before they decay
idea: First principle: if data lives for less than the guaranteed retention (64 ms, with a median of seconds), refreshing it is pure waste. Patch an open accelerator runtime and an FPGA HBM/DDR5 controller so activations, in-flight gradients and per-step scratch go to banks that get no per-bank REF commands. A hardware 32 ms age watchdog turns refresh back on if any page outlives its lease. About $600k and 18 months of engineering.
why: AI working sets are dominated by short-lived tensors. Suppressing refresh on half the banks returns ~5-10% bandwidth and half the refresh energy at 32-64 Gb densities (fact 3), with zero fab changes.

title: Compiler-certified weight re-reads replace refresh during LLM decoding
idea: Every activation is a full restore, and an LLM decode step streams all weights every ~10-50 ms. Add a pass to an open compiler (TVM, Triton or XLA) that proves each weight row is re-read within 32 ms, reordering layer streams if needed. It hands the memory controller a manifest to drop REF for those banks. A small team can demonstrate it on an FPGA accelerator testbed for under $1M in 18 months.
why: Weights fill 60-80% of inference memory, so suppressing their refresh removes most of the 10-20% refresh bandwidth loss and its energy (fact 3).

title: Retention-reject die salvage with per-row refresh controller cards
idea: A die that fails a 64 ms retention screen usually fails because of a few hundred rows, not the whole die. Buy retention-downbinned DRAM at scrap prices and profile every row at 85 C on ~$50k FPGA testers. Sell CXL or DIMM cards whose controller refreshes the weak ~0.1% of rows at 16 ms and the rest at 64 ms. $1M covers testers, the controller FPGA image and first inventory within 24 months.
why: Adds usable bits from existing fabs at near-zero capital, recovering perhaps 1-3% of output that is scrapped or sold into low-grade markets today (supply, capital intensity, fact 3).

title: Arrhenius leakage odometer schedules refresh by integrated charge loss
idea: Leakage scales as exp(-Ea/kT), so integrate a per-module charge-loss budget, the integral of exp(-Ea/kT(t)) dt, from DIMM thermal-sensor samples. Measure each module's Ea at boot by timing first failures at two temperatures. Refresh when the integral reaches the equivalent of 64 ms at 85 C. Controller firmware plus validation costs well under $1M and 12 months.
why: With Ea ~0.6 eV, a DIMM at 50 C leaks ~8x less, and at 40 C ~16x less, than in the 85 C case the spec assumes. Refresh energy and bandwidth fall 5-10x in typical fleets (fact 3).

title: Full-restore sweep banks maximum charge before long idle periods
idea: Retention is t = dQ/I, and timing-limited activations often leave cells ~5-10% short of full VDD. Before a rank enters relaxed refresh or self-refresh, the controller sweeps every row with 2-3x tRAS/tWR so each cell banks its full charge, and only then lengthens the interval. This is pure controller timing work, prototyped on an FPGA DRAM platform for <$200k.
why: Raising the restored level from ~0.9 to ~1.0 VDD adds ~30% margin above the sense threshold, buying 20-40% longer refresh intervals for one cheap sweep (facts 1, 3).

title: Post-package repair as a scalpel for the retention tail
idea: DDR4 and DDR5 already expose soft and hard post-package repair for hard faults. Repurpose it: profile in the field, remap the few rows per bank whose retention is below 256 ms onto spare rows, and run the module at 2-4x tREFI with ECC and patrol scrub as a safety net. Needs BIOS/BMC firmware and a validation lab, ~$400k over 18 months.
why: The refresh interval is dictated by a ~1e-6 fraction of cells. Removing that fraction moves the interval toward median retention (seconds) on existing parts (fact 3); the spare-row count caps how far this goes.

title: Z-channel asymmetric codes match one-directional decay errors
idea: Physics says retention errors go only one way: charged cells lose charge and never gain it. After true/anti-cell mapping, every decay error is therefore a charged-to-empty flip. Implement an asymmetric (Z-channel) error-correcting code, such as Varshamov-Tenengolts or a constant-weight-augmented BCH, in an FPGA controller; it needs about half the parity of a symmetric code. Extend refresh until the decay BER reaches the code's budget. Fits $1M and 24 months.
why: Running at 4-8x longer refresh with ~3-6% parity overhead cuts refresh energy and bandwidth loss in proportion (fact 3).

title: Allocator-driven row refresh: never refresh empty memory
idea: Disable auto-refresh on an FPGA/CXL memory controller and issue targeted ACT-PRE refreshes only for rows backing allocated pages. The kernel's buddy allocator updates the bitmap of allocated rows through a doorbell register. Freed pages are simply abandoned and zeroed on reallocation. Kernel plus controller code costs ~$300k over 12 months.
why: Refresh energy scales with rows refreshed, and fleet memory is often 30-50% free or reclaimable, so about that fraction of refresh energy and REF bandwidth comes back (fact 3).

title: Sacrificial canary rows give closed-loop refresh margin
idea: Profile each channel's 64 weakest rows at boot, fill them with known patterns, and refresh them 1.5x less often than data rows. Poll them every interval, so the first canary flip (from a temperature spike or VRT jump) immediately tightens the refresh rate for data rows. Controller firmware and validation cost under $300k.
why: Worst-case guardbanding becomes feedback, so data runs near its measured retention (2-4x the spec interval) on commodity parts (fact 3), at a cost of a few rows per channel.

title: Decay-tolerant page cache re-faults from flash instead of refreshing
idea: Clean pages (file cache, model weights loaded from NVMe, read-only container layers) have an authoritative copy on storage, so they need probable, not guaranteed, retention. Keep them in banks at 8x relaxed refresh with a per-line CRC. On a mismatch the kernel drops the page and re-faults it from storage. A kernel patch plus controller CRC fits easily within $1M and 18 months.
why: Clean pages often fill 30-60% of server DRAM; cutting their refresh 8x removes a large share of refresh energy (fact 3) at no capacity cost.

title: Polarity-aware scrambling keeps most cells in the uncharged state
idea: Only charged cells decay, and 'charged' means '1' in true cells and '0' in anti-cells. Learn each row's true/anti layout with a one-time retention test. Then XOR each 64 B line with that map, plus a per-line inversion bit chosen to minimize charged cells, so zero-heavy data leaves most capacitors empty. Firmware and FPGA work, <$300k.
why: The charged-cell fraction drops from ~50% to ~10-40% depending on data. Decay-error rate falls in proportion, so ECC-backed refresh intervals can stretch further (fact 3).

title: Bit-plane split refresh: exponents guarded, low mantissa bits relaxed
idea: Bits do not carry equal information: a flipped low mantissa bit in bfloat16 perturbs a value by <2^-4 relative, while an exponent flip can be catastrophic. Transpose KV-cache and activation tensors into bit-planes. Sign, exponent and the top 3 mantissa bits go in normally refreshed banks; the low 4 mantissa bits go in banks refreshed 8-16x less. Validate on open LLMs with a ~$150k software and FPGA effort.
why: Relaxing refresh 8x on a quarter of KV-cache bits trims ~20% of its refresh energy with <6% error per value (fact 3).

title: Image-sensor foundry dark pixels as long-retention memory cells
idea: CMOS image sensors fight exactly DRAM's leakage physics (SRH generation) and win: pinned photodiodes reach dark currents of ~1-10 electrons/s (~1e-18 A), against DRAM's 13 fA tail. Tape out a $200-300k MPW in a CIS process with light-shielded 4T pixels repurposed as memory. The pinned diode stores ~5,000 electrons written by fill-and-spill through the transfer gate, the transfer gate is the access device, and the floating diffusion with source follower gives a gain readout.
why: ~1e4x lower leakage means minutes of retention at room temperature. The tapeout is a cheap testbed for pinned-storage-node physics in future DRAM cells and a refresh-free macro for U.S. CIS lines (fact 3, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Open BMC retention telemetry builds per-part-number refresh tables
idea: Ship an open-source BMC agent that logs corrected-error addresses, DIMM temperatures and part/lot numbers, and runs a 2-minute monthly retention probe on one drained rank. Pool anonymized data across operators into a public per-lot retention model that publishes safe tREFI tables with quantified risk. Software plus a small data team, <$700k over 24 months.
why: Spec refresh is set by the worst lot of the worst vendor; statistics over 100k+ DIMMs justify 2-4x relaxation for most lots (fact 3).

title: Uncorrectable-error insurance underwrites relaxed-refresh deployments
idea: Operators won't run DRAM outside spec because a rare uncorrectable error is an unpriced tail risk. Form a small underwriting venture that prices that risk from controlled retention-stress data and fleet telemetry. It sells per-server policies that pay out on detected uncorrectable errors for customers running certified extended-refresh settings. The actuarial model, test lab and a reinsurer partnership fit within $1M and 24 months.
why: This turns a technical guardband (2-4x refresh margin) into a financial one, unlocking 2-4x refresh savings in fleets that would never adopt them unhedged (fact 3).

title: Power-gate idle ranks once idle time beats the break-even
idea: Compute the break-even from first principles. A 64 GB DDR5 RDIMM in self-refresh burns ~0.5 W, while spilling and restoring 64 GB to NVMe costs ~2 nJ/B each way (~250 J), so any idle stretch beyond ~8 minutes is cheaper with the rank powered off. Add a hypervisor policy that compacts cold pages, spills them to NVMe or compresses them into active ranks, and cuts the rank's rails through the DIMM PMIC. Software and firmware, <$500k.
why: This removes retention energy entirely for idle capacity (overnight and diurnal troughs), attacking refresh's 16-33% share of idle power across the data center (fact 3).

title: 22FDX eDRAM with back-gate retention bias on a U.S. line
idea: Fully depleted SOI gives every transistor an independent back gate with a ~80 mV/V body factor. Tape out a 1T1C (MIM-capacitor) eDRAM macro on GlobalFoundries 22FDX in Malta, NY via MPW. The array's back-gate well swings to -2 V during retention, raising access Vt ~160 mV, and returns to 0 V during access. MPW, design and test fit ~$700k over 20 months.
why: +160 mV of Vt at ~70 mV/dec cuts hold-state subthreshold leakage ~200x while keeping access current. It demonstrates refresh-light, DRAM-class embedded memory on a U.S. fab (fact 3, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Shortened-tRCD reads act as a non-destructive charge gauge
idea: A cell's remaining charge sets how fast its bitline develops, so reading a row with a deliberately shortened tRCD fails first on the cells that have leaked most. The sense amplifier still restores the row correctly. Probe rows this way periodically, then re-read at nominal timing for the real data, to build a live per-row charge-margin map and give each row its own refresh interval. FPGA controller work, ~$250k.
why: Online profiling that preserves data gets around the VRT problem that makes static profiles unsafe, enabling per-row refresh at 2-4x the average interval (fact 3).

title: Second-life DDR4 behind CXL controllers with per-row refresh
idea: Hyperscalers retire millions of DDR4 RDIMMs that still work but whose retention tails have aged. Build a CXL Type-3 FPGA card that hosts eight retired DIMMs, profiles every row at intake, and runs per-row refresh plus strong ECC. Sell it as a far-memory tier; the prototype and pilot run fit within $1M and 24 months.
why: Adds usable capacity without new wafers (supply, capital and scarce-resource axes), with refresh tuned to measured retention rather than spec (fact 3).

title: High-pressure deuterium anneal of purchased finished DRAM wafers
idea: Interface and dangling-bond traps near storage junctions drive SRH tail leakage, and Si-D bonds resist depassivation better than Si-H. Buy finished DRAM wafers or known-good-die lots, run 20 atm D2 anneals at 350-400 C in a rented high-pressure furnace, and measure the retention-tail shift against control wafers. ~$300-500k including test, 15 months.
why: If the tail compresses even 2x, vendors can adopt a single back-end anneal step for 2x longer refresh (fact 3).

title: Retention-DLTS fingerprints the defect species behind the leakage tail
idea: Treat a commodity DRAM as a billion-pixel deep-level transient spectrometer. Measure each weak cell's retention time against temperature (the Arrhenius slope gives trap energy) and against wordline/plate bias (the field-enhancement factor separates Poole-Frenkel, phonon-assisted tunneling and GIDL). Cluster the signatures across vendors and lots to name the dominant defect species (Fe-B, vacancy-oxygen, interface Pb centers).
why: Knowing which defect sets the 13 fA tail tells fabs which fix (gettering, passivation or field relief) buys the most refresh relief. A two-person lab with FPGA testers and thermal chambers can do it for <$500k in 18 months (fact 3).

title: JEDEC retention-class mode register lets controllers trust each die
idea: Propose and fund a JEDEC ballot that adds a mode-register field where each die reports its own tested retention class per bank (64, 128, 256 or 512 ms at 85 C) from production test. Add a 'relaxed refresh permitted' bit tied to the vendor's warranty. $1M funds reference characterization data, a compliant FPGA controller and two years of standards work.
why: Vendors already measure retention but throw the result away into a worst-case spec. Exposing it lets every controller run at the die's real interval, a fleet-wide 2-4x cut in refresh overhead (fact 3).

title: Best-effort memory cloud instances priced like spot capacity
idea: Offer a cloud instance class whose memory runs at 4-8x relaxed refresh, optionally on salvaged or second-life DRAM, at ~40% lower price. Guests see it as 'best-effort RAM' with a poison-page signal. Target workloads that checkpoint or recompute, such as ML training with frequent checkpoints, caches and batch analytics. A neocloud can pilot it on a few racks for <$1M within 24 months.
why: Turns the retention guardband into a priced product tier, lowering the effective cost per usable bit and stretching scarce DRAM supply (fact 3, cost per bit).
